name: The example
expr: [('-inf' if x == float('-inf') else x) for x in cheapest(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2])]
why: [0, 1, 2, 4, 2]. The refund on 2 → 1 makes 0 → 2 → 1 cost 2 − 1 = 1, less than the direct 4.

name: Dijkstra's method is wrong here
expr: [('-inf' if x == float('-inf') else x) for x in cheapest(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2])]
why: [0, 1, 3, 2]. Dijkstra's method settles 1 at 2 (the nearest), then 3 at 3, and only then finds 0 → 2 → 1 for 1. Its answers for 1 and 3 are too big (lesson 3).

name: Stations that cannot be reached
expr: [('-inf' if x == float('-inf') else x) for x in cheapest(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2])]
why: [0, 5, None, None]: nothing leads from 0 to 2 or 3.

name: A loop of refunds
expr: [('-inf' if x == float('-inf') else x) for x in cheapest(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2])]
why: [0, '-inf', '-inf', '-inf', None]. The loop 1 → 2 → 1 costs −2 each time round, so 1, 2 and everything after them can be made as cheap as you like: -math.inf (shown here as '-inf'). 4 cannot be reached at all.

name: A loop of refunds that cannot be reached
expr: [('-inf' if x == float('-inf') else x) for x in cheapest(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2])]
why: [0, 3, 4, None, None]. The loop 3 → 4 → 3 costs −4, but the start cannot reach it, so it changes nothing.

name: A cheap way that a loop beats later
expr: [('-inf' if x == float('-inf') else x) for x in cheapest(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2])]
why: [0, '-inf', '-inf', '-inf', '-inf', '-inf']. After n − 1 rounds, 5 still has −50 from the direct line, and the extra round does not lower it: the loop has not gone round often enough yet. But the loop can be used again and again, so 5 has no lowest fare either. Mark the stations that still improve in the extra round, then everything they can reach (lesson 4).

name: The start is on the loop
expr: [('-inf' if x == float('-inf') else x) for x in cheapest(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2])]
why: ['-inf', '-inf', '-inf']: even the start can be reached for less and less.

name: A loop that costs exactly 0
expr: [('-inf' if x == float('-inf') else x) for x in cheapest(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2])]
why: [0, 2, -1, 0]. Going round 1 → 2 → 1 costs 0, which saves nothing. Only loops that cost less than 0 make fares fall without limit.

name: 1,000 stations, 3,000 fares and a chain
expr: (lambda o: [len(o), o.count(None), o.count('-inf'), sum(x for x in o if type(x) is int) % 1000000007, o[:6]])([('-inf' if x == float('-inf') else x) for x in cheapest(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2])])
show: 1,000 stations, 3,000 random fares among the first 900 (many negative, no loop below 0), plus a chain 0 → 1 → … → 999 listed from the far end
why: [how many, how many None, how many '-inf', a check number, the first six]. The chain is listed backwards, so each round moves its fares on by one station: about 1,000 rounds of 4,000 fares. Stop early when a round changes nothing.

name: The same with a loop of refunds
expr: (lambda o: [len(o), o.count(None), o.count('-inf'), sum(x for x in o if type(x) is int) % 1000000007, o[:6]])([('-inf' if x == float('-inf') else x) for x in cheapest(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2])])
show: the network above, plus a loop 950 → 951 → 950 on the chain that costs −100
why: [how many, how many None, how many '-inf', a check number, the first six]. Stations 950 to 999 have no lowest fare: the loop can reach them. The loop cannot reach the others, so they keep their fares.
